Our analysis focuses on the duration of Abelian gauge fields within an AdS five-dimensional space using the Fierz transformation to identify the most effective choice of quark combinations within the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay. We determined the most favorable quark combinations that yield the longest decay duration by calculating the dual field strengths using the Fierz transformation, which leads to a calculation of the decay duration. Our results indicate the most efficient quark combinations that result in the longest decay duration of approximately $0.42\cdot10^{-12}s$.

This research paper examines a significant innovation in solving a discrete time-state control issue with a stochastic differential equation component. We introduce a new approach to approximate the optimal control strategy and associated cost value. Previously proposed approximation methods are compared to our novel approach via numerical examples set in finance and finance-related optimization problems. We also examine the convergence properties of our new method.

Our investigation focused on identifying patterns of polarization resulting from the scattering of extremely energetic cosmic rays interacting with atmospheric particles at the Pierre Auger Observatory. Through our analysis, we applied optimized methods to our data and compared them with theoretical predictions from the arrival directions and orientations of cosmic rays, taking into account various physical scenarios. Our findings were expressed in terms of the power spectra of polarization patterns, and we further examined them in relation to cosmic rays' energy and tilt properties. Our data revealed that the patterns of polarization exhibited a linear relationship with the energy of the cosmic rays, with an estimated value of 1.15 ± 0.25 (stat) ± 0.15 (syst) × 10^-3 (GeV/ln GeV) when considering the most comprehensive dataset, with an associated significance of 5.5σ. We also analyzed specific subsets of arrival directions, including those from the celestial equator, the Galactic Center, and the anomalous gamma-ray excess region in the Galactic Center. Furthermore, we investigated the tilt properties of cosmic rays within these regions. Our research revealed that the patterns of polarization exhibited varying relationships with the energy of the cosmic rays in these areas, with the patterns of polarization also influenced by the tilt properties in some cases.

This paper proves that any finite dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses the characteristic property of being solvable, thereby extending the scope of a previously established Russian result to a broader, more specific algebraic context.

Our research delves into the analysis of flow direction and flow intensity across various centralities in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC's 5.02 TeV energy level. By correlating charged particles with the second- and fourth-order harmonic flow, we determined the coefficients that characterize flow direction and flow intensity. Subsequently, these coefficients were utilized to derive the average flow direction and intensity in each centrality range. Our findings revealed that the average flow direction exhibits little change from semi-peripheral collisions to central collisions, while the average flow intensity demonstrates a notable increase with decreasing centrality. Furthermore, the ratio of average flow intensity to initial geometric eccentricity achieves unity in central collisions, thereby meeting the necessary condition for the conceptualization of non-equilibrium initial conditions within hydrodynamic models.

The process of comparing and integrating identical-shaped tables that
contain functional relationships and entries with unknown values is a complex
task. We have demonstrated that even when the number of missing values is
substantial, certain types of functional comparisons can be efficiently
computed using linear algebra. Furthermore, we found that the quality of the
integrated data can be significantly improved by employing a broad range of
comparison functions that encompass popular options like the intersection,
union, and set difference, as well as more sophisticated options like the
Wasserstein and Earth movers distances. As evidenced by our experiments, the
best comparison function varies greatly depending on the specific dataset,
and several strategies for selecting the optimal function have been demonstrated
through our research. A notable finding is that both the number of missing
values and the specific comparison function exert equal influences on the
improvement in data integration quality.

To effectively manage and prevent overflows in network systems, researchers typically study and compare different data processing models. Among various models compared through simulations in this research, a novel TVPAR model outperforms the existing PAR model in both average and 95th percentile values for various metrics including queue length, overflow frequency, and average processing time.

We introduce NDF-Net: a novel neural network architecture called Neural Description Fields, capable of capturing the essence of objects within 3D point clouds that are subject to rigid transformations. This novel framework redefines object representations using probability distributions over 3D spaces, tied to specific reference frames. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on orientation-agnostic descriptions, these representations retain their equivariant properties through transformations. As a result, corresponding features remain invariant, ensuring that objects' essential characteristics are preserved across different viewpoints. We further develop an innovative training method, known as equivariant contrastive learning, which leverages the contrastive multiset contrast loss from [2] in conjunction with spatial equivariance loss, to train NDF-Net for object classification and detection within 3D point clouds. Moreover, we demonstrate a novel way to incorporate these representations into traditional detection frameworks, enabling the direct utilization of NDF-Net. Our results show that NDF-Net achieves superior performance on ModelNet40 and SUN3D datasets, surpassing the current state-of-the-art on 40-class classification and ranking second on SUN3D classification, while ranking first on SUN3D detection.

Using the functional renormalization group at the long-wavelength limit, we have the results for Yang-Lee edges in O(N)>1 and O(N)=1 models. Within the context of O(N) universality classes in three dimensions, these outcomes indicate the positions of Yang-Lee edges in model space. Specifically, Yang-Lee edges in the 3D $XY$ model ($N=1$) and the 3D Heisenberg model ($N \to \infty$) are mapped out. The focus is on Yang-Lee edge criticality and the positions of reference trajectories that cross the edge critically at $h=0$ in field space. The locations are described in terms of the order parameter field $\phi$ as $N \to \infty$ yields an edge curve while $N=1$ yields a edge critical line. The design of the parameter space is based on the presence of the gradient term in the effective action.

In statistics and machine learning, an important problem is to analyze the behavior of an optimization procedure on a single instance of the training data. To this end, we develop a new approach based on the Self-Consistent Approximate Mean-Field theory, which allows us to characterize the stability of the solution and estimate the out-of-sample performance within the setting of convex minimization without incurring an exponential growth in the number of parameters included in the model.

The Spellar project aims to create a sophisticated approach for assessing aerosol density via photometric analysis in visible spectra, building on the concept of a stellar atmosphere model. By comparing observed spectra to simulated data based on the Mie scattering pattern of specific aerosol types, we can determine their density. A novel method using likelihood estimation forms the foundation of our analysis, which compares observed data to modeled outcomes via the chi-squared statistical test. By evaluating various model parameters and assessing model fit through polynomial regression, we can derive an empirical formula for estimating aerosol density. A simulation involving synthetic data showed that even with limited spectral resolution, accurate aerosol density estimates can be achieved, with an RMS error of 1.1 overall.

We present the Dark Room with a Hole (DeepHMap++) approach, an innovative method for estimating a 6-DoF object pose in cluttered environments with multiple objects by analyzing a single monochrome image. Our technique performs a 2D projection space clustering of object models' features and directly learns correspondences between model projections and image regions without relying on 2D detection or feature extraction. A robust estimator calculates the pose parameters based on the clustered projections and their corresponding image regions. We demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed method by conducting experiments on the BV-MIO-Map dataset and the HPB-MIO-Map dataset, achieving superior performance in both cases.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based library for Generalized Graphical Lasso
techniques. Based on the original work of (Friedman, 2008), we adapted the
algorithm to handle data with a non-Euclidean structure, specifically for
Euclidean, symmetric positive definite matrix-valued, and directed graphical
models. These variations involve distinct penalty functions, such as the
Frobenius, matrix trace, and log-determinant, which are derived from the
underlying distribution of the data. These choices influence the optimization
problem, which we address using an iterative algorithm, specifically the
Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers. We demonstrate the efficacy of
our implementation by conducting simulations and real-world data analysis
experiments.

Numerous methodologies are being developed to accelerate molecular configurational sampling in molecular dynamics simulations. By applying an appropriate strategy of this kind, simulations can be completed more quickly while still producing highly accurate results for binding free energies and other properties that rely on precise calculations of configurational thermodynamics. Our research involves testing and evaluating two established methods: the use of multiple time steps in the Langevin dynamics algorithm and the application of our previously developed "configurational bias" technique. We demonstrated that combining these two methods leads to a significant reduction in the number of configurational samples required while maintaining the same level of precision in calculations of average configurational energies. In particular, when binding free energies are being calculated, we found that using an optimized combination of these methods can lead to a 6-fold decrease in the number of configurational samples needed, to the benefit of researchers who rely on our previous research for their own purposes.

Our new method measures the significance of nodes in multilayer networks by evaluating the change in eigenvectors when removing nodes, taking into account the distinction between layers. Unlike existing approaches that treat layers as individual entities when calculating the significance of nodes, our method considers the interconnectivity between layers. As a result, we can determine the most prominent nodes across all layers and identify those that contribute significantly to the overall structure of the network. Furthermore, our approach enables the construction of a simplified model of multilayer networks by removing the most insignificant nodes in each layer. We have tested our method on various multilayer networks, including those related to biology, finance, and transportation, and our results show that the most prominent nodes are often located at the interface between layers. Additionally, we found that our method can effectively identify the most critical nodes in complex systems by comparing the eigenvectors of original and randomized networks.

We examine the $R$-Minkowski spacetime metric, which is characterized by a single free parameter and is based on the concept of relative time. We then derive the geometric interpretation of the Schr\"{o}dinger equation within this spacetime framework.

This study utilizes high-speed imaging to examine spheres interacting with a plane water surface, specifically in the moderate regime (0.5-3 m/s) where the seal response is most complex. A well-defined groove forms at the water surface as the spheres move through it, yet the seal area remains variable and is influenced by the drag regime, sphere size, and surface roughness. The results reveal that spheres in the intermediate drag regime exhibit the largest seal areas, while those in the transitional regime have the smallest. Furthermore, the formation of the groove and surrounding roughness can lead to spheres becoming stuck, despite efforts to make the surface smooth. The stickiness is mitigated by increasing speed, reducing surface roughness, or using larger spheres.

To investigate the role of symmetries in string theory at high-energy scales, we analyze Type IIB string theory in a compactified torus with D7-branes. Initially, we establish that a specific set of Weyl rescalings is made up of conformal symmetry components. Consequently, conformal symmetry is either completely destroyed or remaining in a weakened form, depending on specific calibration properties being met. To recover a more robust symmetry, we are forced to expand the theta-term parameters to include higher-order terms in the Calabi-Yau form expansion. In doing so, we uncover the universal criteria that these expanded terms must satisfy in order to maintain holomorphic symmetry. Furthermore, we find that a particular set of monomial operators can be generated from the expanded theta-term parameters through a holomorphic symmetry transformation procedure.

Our calculations using first-principles methods have examined the orbital occupancy in cubanite, specifically the 3d energy levels of iron within two-ferric spinel structures. By comparing with an isolated iron atom reference, we found significant differences in calculations of occupancy weights using either the cubic or tetrahedral spinel structure assumptions. In the assumed tetrahedral structure, our results align with previous experimental interpretations of x-ray absorption spectroscopy data, providing insight into the material's electronic properties and potential lattice distortions within the compound.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum systems like ultra-coordinated Rydberg atoms and massive, long-lived nuclear magneto-electric moments hold great promise in this area. However, these systems often require sophisticated technology for implementation and typically operate at a slow pace due to their large sizes and long-lived lifetimes. In contrast, semiconductor quantum dots exhibit rapid dynamics and are technologically well-developed, yet they often fall short of ultra-coordination. Our research utilizes a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental results to demonstrate the interplay between light, electron spins, and lattice vibrations in semiconductor quantum dots. By adjusting inter-particle distances and inter-particle interactions, we found that even in the presence of pure dephasing, there is a threshold for external light forcing that leads to large-scale oscillations between a bright exciton and a dark exciton state. When this threshold is met, the dark exciton state becomes resistant to destruction by environments, identifying it as a 'quantum hidden state.' Furthermore, our results indicate that in a system of two quantum dots, long-lasting dark exciton states and their resistance to external forcing and environment degradation can be achieved without the need for a magnetic field, which is typically required for this effect.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D wall paper material lattice within the non-symmorphic 21719 symmetry group. By integrating an in-plane electric field, we found it can modify the symmetry of this material to a non-symmorphic 4-fold rotation around a specific axis, a 2-fold rotation around a perpendicular axis, and a mirror reflection across a plane perpendicular to another axis. As a result, this material enters a topological insulator state with helical Dirac cones that can be manipulated by an external magnetic field. Under such a condition, we identify six possible location configurations for the helical cones, and couple them to light within a 2D photonic crystal construction. By combining a microcavity and photonic crystal construction, we generate an engineered environment where the helical cones can switch between being inside or outside energy gaps of the middle band, resulting in tunable coupling to either an electric or magnetic near-field within the microcavity.

Building upon the principle of quantum-optical catalysis, where the interaction between a beam and a cavity is used to convert single photons into coherent states, we examine the case where the beam contains multiple photons. We investigate the conditions under which the central photon within a facilitated state maintains its original properties, and analyze the resulting state to determine its quantum characteristics. Furthermore, we explore the consequences of losing photons during transmission within an optical system.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. Specifically, under the assumption of vanishing cosmological constant, a comprehensive analysis is performed to determine the bivector components that allow for the existence of solutions to Einstein's field equations in conjunction with specific matter field theories. A detailed examination is undertaken for each of the following cases: electromagnetic fields, conformally flat spaces, cavities surrounded by a perfect fluid, perfect fluid systems, and various algebraic classifications of the Weyl tensor.

Our proposed method uses the structure of a program to inform deductions about 
its constituent parts, applying this insight to polymers and Boolean formulas. 
Given a function f and input values x1, x2, we deduce the value of f(x1, x2) 
based on the source code of f. Our technique involves three steps: 
identifying relevant code, computing a feature vector, and making a prediction. 
These steps are applied to a linear regression setting and a SAT solver case 
study, demonstrating the benefits of our approach by comparing it to standard 
methods and random search.

We present a novel medical image segmentation technique, dubbed Dense Focus Unet, which we have applied to an intricate task like esophageal tumor identification and extraction from CT scans. This model, with two variants, has been used to achieve both segmentation and object removal within the esophagus. We have developed a specific dataset, comprising 200 CT scans with accurately annotated tumors, to train and test the model. To evaluate the model's performance, we used 50 CT scans from a public source, and the remaining 150 scans constitute our training and validation data. The DDAUnet model achieved a score of 0.75 on the public dataset and 0.83 on our private dataset, based on the metric of Dice Similarity Coefficient.

Code-mixed languages, combining two or more languages within a word or sentence structure, are a prevalent form of communication used by multilingual speakers to convey identity, community, and cultural aspects. As a result, there is a growing interest in NLP research that considers code-mixed languages, with studies examining topics such as language choice, code-mixing patterns, and implications for multilingual individuals' cognitive development, group dynamics, social relationships, and how they present themselves to the public. Additionally, code-mixed languages have been explored in NLP tasks and applications, including sentiment analysis, paraphrasing, machine translation, summarization, and question answering. However, there are several obstacles facing the development of effective NLP models for code-mixed languages, including a lack of large-scale high-quality datasets, inadequate representation learning techniques, and limited consideration of linguistic aspects, cultural elements, and individual differences. As a result, current models struggle to generalize to new data and tasks, and more research is necessary to fully leverage the linguistic complexity and cultural richness of code-mixed languages.

The metric used to evaluate image description systems is continuously evolving,
driven by improvements in computer vision and neural language processing.
Describing images that are dissimilar requires a more nuanced method,
one that distinguishes between difficult images and those with inadequate
databases. The proposal to employ references with varied descriptions for a
single image was recently introduced. In this paper, an alternate approach is
explored: utilizing a single description for each image. This choice enables the
computation of a more precise metric that reflects the complex relationship
between the image, the model, and the description. Experimental results on the
SHAWDOW dataset demonstrate the benefits of this approach, specifically the
 discovery of a stronger correlation between the existing metric and human scores
obtained through crowdsourcing. Additionally, this approach leads to a more
precise estimation of the relationship between the image and the model, without
overfitting.

We employed and combined DFT and Monte Carlo methods to investigate the electronic and structural properties of tantalum oxide, with particular focus on its bulk and thin-film aspects. Through relaxation of bulk Ta$_2$O$_5$ within the DFT framework, we identified two possible oxygen layers that can terminate the surface. Subsequent MC simulations revealed that both surface terminations are energetically equivalent, despite differing lattice parameters. Furthermore, we found that Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibits a stable passivation state without significant reaction or segregation in thin films. Through MC simulations, we were able to determine the passivation state's characteristics, which include the formation of oxygen vacancies and metal-dimer formation within the Ta$_2$O$_5$ films.

Our analysis of Reddit user interactions across the United States identifies a large-scale network pattern called the Big Geographic Arrangement (BGA), which consists of isolated regions of highly interconnected users and is characterized by a significant disparity in connectivity levels. We examined the BGA's impact on the spread of misinformation within this user base by synthetically introducing false information and tracking its transmission. Our findings reveal that the BGA's distinct features significantly contribute to the identification of misinformation sources by highlighting regions with unusually high amounts of externally-derived information and low connectivity with nearby areas. We validated our approach using real-world propaganda examples and observed a 10-30% decrease in detection errors when considering the BGA, and a 25-50% decrease in detection errors when the condition on external information is added. Moreover, we found that removing the most centrally located user in a component does not substantially affect the remaining users' trust in the information, which has important implications for modeling real-world networks.

As robots become part of our daily environment, understanding their auditory feedback is crucial to ensure safety and effective operation. Research indicates that auditory feedback via speech and other sounds for robots can be both socially and technologically beneficial when designed properly. Nonetheless, developing suitable auditory feedback requires knowledge of human speech patterns, particularly how instructors narrate their actions to robots via speech. To this end, a novel approach is proposed to extract vital features from instruction speech by leveraging convolutional neural networks. Subsequent application of recurrent neural networks in a multi-step process is used to forecast future speech segments. Together, these networks can accurately predict instruction speech patterns even when started in the middle of an audio sequence. The proposed method is demonstrated through a series of experiments using actual audio data. Additionally, an interesting finding related to speech prediction is observed, which could be valuable for ongoing task detection or other purposes.

We explore the concept of intricacy in geometric field theory through the Euler-Arnold equations, building on the fundamental work by Geometric field theory researchers. Intricacy is characterized as the rate at which a field becomes disorganized. By applying Lighthill's classification, we examine the intricacy of fields within three categories: solvable, solvable but not integrable, and non-smooth scenarios.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and companies like Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and IBM are competing to provide superior customer interactions. To compare their performance, evaluating conversational systems is crucial. Although existing assessment methods are multi-faceted, they often require substantial manual effort to operate. In response, we present a programable, fully-automated evaluation framework called Converse, which leverages multiple assessment methods, real-time user feedback, and customizable evaluation criteria. Converse is designed with a user-friendly interface that allows system developers to configure testing scenarios, recruit test users, monitor interactions, and analyze feedback. Furthermore, the framework provides extensive tools for testing scenario development, user feedback analysis, system evaluation, and comparison, all of which can be tailored to meet diverse needs. By providing a versatile, automated evaluation framework, we give system developers the ability to compare their systems' performance and identify areas for improvement.

Cross-domain recommendation has been a highly sought-after technology for 
addressing the data sparsity and diversity challenges encountered in recommender systems.
Multiple sparse domains have been tackled by tending toward a single target domain,
yet this approach isn't practical due to the diversity of domains encountered in real-world applications.
In this paper, a novel method called multi-sparse-domain cooperative recommendation is proposed.
In this proposed method, multiple target domains are considered at the same time.
The cooperatives recommendation method learns about the aspects and weights of each domain.
A thorough aspect preference learning framework is then established to conduct collaborative learning among the domains.
Within this framework, a thorough aspect preference learning framework is developed to conduct collaborative learning among the domains.
Through experiments using real data, the effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated.
The proposed method is compared against both single-target and multi-target domain recommendation approaches.
In addition to this, the impact of diverse domains is examined through an artificial data creation process.
The proposed method's ability to handle diverse domains is also examined.
The proposed method reduces data sparsity by transferring knowledge among the domains.
The proposed method also reduces diversity by targeting multiple domains at once.
In this way, the proposed method overcomes both data sparsity and diversity challenges.
A big advantage of the proposed method is that the proposed method doesn't join the target domains together.
As a result of this, the proposed method is suitable for a wide range of real-world applications.

Conic optimization problems expressed over convex cones have wide-ranging applications in data analysis, machine learning, finance, and more. Many real-world problems require the resolution of dehomogenized conic problems due to variables being expressed on non-traditional scales. Despite the "easy" transformation, standard conic solvers struggle with variable scaling issues, making specialized techniques like bounds and barrier width management essential for their effectiveness. We present Hypatia, a high-performance solver for dehomogenized conic problems that leverages JuMP and MOSEK to provide an interface for an expansive collection of conic formulations and their resolution, along with scaling-aware strategies for problem parameters and variable scaling. We showcase Hypatia's capabilities in addressing NLP conic formulations and the resolution of organic conic formulations in the DeHom-CCGI dataset.

The escalating use and reliance on MRI in clinical settings necessitate quality control to ensure image data meets high standards for diagnostic accuracy. As automated image acquisition systems become more prevalent, quality control is shifting from a manual process to one that is partially automated, presenting a significant challenge. In this context, learning-based methods are emerging as a promising solution to tackle quality assurance in MRI. However, such methods require a high level of dimensionality in input data, including spatial and frequency domains, fused feature maps from deep neural networks, that hinders generalization to new, unseen situations. This could a result of artificial dependencies created between dimensions that hinder the model's ability to recognize essential features, thus making it difficult for the model to generalize to new, similar situations. This research leverages multi-dimensional generalization ability of learning regulators, specifically multi-task learning, density-based clustering, and transfer learning, to tackle MRI quality assurance as a complex issue of this nature. The proposed framework is applied to two concrete problems: removing artifacts in MRI images and evaluating the quality of MRI images. Experimental results show that this approach yields superior performance compared to current standards in artifact removal and MRI image assessment quality metrics.

To analyze the impact of private EVs on power grid stability, a multi-agent optimization model was developed which considers the interconnection between electrical and energy systems. The model breaks down large problems into manageable scales by representing agents, resources, and facilities as separate entities. These entities interact with each other through complex relationships defined by individual purposes, constraints, and incentive mechanisms. A decomposition-coordination method was utilized to solve a centralized problem that accounts for the autonomy of agents, and simulations were conducted using a randomly generated sample of 500 private EV owners and 10 charging stations. The results showed that optimizing individual purposes and incentive mechanisms individually can lead to a stable equilibrium, and that charging stations located in areas with higher population density tend to exhibit greater volatility.

In multi-agent meetings, where multiple autonomous entities collaborate
through discussion, the order of actions taken by the agents is often
determined by their individual interests. We refer to the sequence of actions
as the "drive" of the meeting. Our research focuses on designing a framework
to identify drives in meetings that involve multiple agents, where the drive
is seen as a key factor in determining the purpose and outcome of the meeting
itself. To achieve this, we developed an automated method to detect drives
in meetings, characterize their objectives, and measure the success of the
meeting based on the achieved goal. Our analysis covers various types of meetings
including those with competing or cooperative agents, and our approach
is demonstrated through applications in sports, finance, and negotiation
scenarios.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of novel tin-based GdCmSn3 and GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds with a cubic skutterudite structure. Using the Bloch theorem and density functional theory, we investigated the fundamental characteristics of these materials with different crystal lattice parameters. Our results show that the optimal lattice constant for these materials is approximately 7.85 Angstroms, leading to a minimal band gap of about 0.05 eV and a curie temperature of about 870 K. Furthermore, our calculations indicate that GdCmSn3 is a half-metallic material with an extremely small band gap at the Fermi level, whereas GdxCm1-xSn3 exhibits a mix of half-metallic and semiconducting behaviors along its compositional line. Our research also reveals unique magnetic properties among the atomic and pair-wise interactions in these materials, which could be useful for understanding their unique characteristics and regulating their magnetic properties.

Using chiral effective theory and quark symmetry, we re-examine quark combinations that result in massless electroweak neutrinos and predict the masses of exotic baryons and mesons within the 1-2 GeV range. We focus on ground-state mesons and baryons that consist of three quarks, three antiquarks, a quark and an antiquark, or a diquark and an antiquark. We also consider both scalar and axial baryons. Calculated masses are compared to existing experimental data and those from lattice QCD.

The Coxeter groups, fueled by their applications in various fields such as physics, geometry, and combinatorics, serve a fundamental purpose in the study and analysis of root systems. Specifically, the invariant operators within these systems, powered by their underlying geometric structure, possess distinct properties that are reflected in the composition and behavior of their characters. The character of the Coxeter system is characterized as a function that maps the operator compositions to scalar values, displaying cyclic symmetry properties rooted in the system's geometry. The Coxeter groups, in their most basic form, consist of a set of generating operators that adhere to specific rules when composed, namely the parabolic relation, which is linked to the system's geometry and notably characterized by the absence of 3-cycles within the b-type Coxeter groups. The foundation theorem, a seminal result, describes the composition of the character function in terms of the defining operators and their exponential equivalents. Building upon the foundational work of Lassalle, we derive a generalized version of the foundation theorem, leveraging the analytic properties of the character function and the geometric properties of the root systems. Through this approach, we obtain an expression for the composition of the character function, tied to the system's geometry and specifically characterized by the absence of 3-cycles within the b-type Coxeter groups.

Using the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and mock catalogs, we calculated weak lensing convergence weights for a sample of Type Ia supernovae based on their distances. Converging weights were calculated through the relation $w \approx \frac{2}{\sigma^2} \left( \frac{\delta_m}{b_\sigma} \right)^2 = \frac{2}{\sigma^2} \left( \frac{\delta_m}{\sigma \sqrt{2}} \right)^2 $, where $\delta_m$ is the dimensionless convergence fluctuation compared to the mean. We found that the distribution of weights is Poisson-distributed, as expected from the superposition of light curves. We investigate T-shaped resonators made up of silicon and air, integrated within a silicon-on-insulator material structure. By employing finite-difference time-domain simulations, we analyze various configurations of the air components and silicon wires to determine their impact on mode characteristics, particularly in the fundamental mode. Our study reveals that a specific design, which includes a curved section of a photonic wire, results in improved mode characteristics, both in terms of size and loss, compared to traditional T-shaped resonators.

For our task, we selected 10 object categories from the MS COCO database –
namely, bird, car, chair, dog, horse, laptop, microphone, plate, sofa,
and tree. We used a subset of COCO images containing these categories,
chosen at random from the 25,000 image set, totaling approximately
10,000 images. To further ensure diversity, we picked 500 images from each
category. Our assessment shows that a top-performing detector like FIO
achieves an AP of only 10% for an unknown object called "deercat," which
is actually a dog, indicating a significant context-related issue. To
investigate the context-related issues, we created a synthetic dataset where
object categories were changed, such as "car" becoming a "tree." Our
experiments on both real and synthetic data revealed the limitations of the
current object detectors and highlighted the importance of considering the
context when detecting objects.

This study focuses on the existence and multiplicity of positive solutions for a specific type of elliptic equation that includes the Kirchhoff functional, which is characterized by the singular Trudinger-Moser growth condition and an inhomogeneous term within the $p$-Laplacian framework. We establish the foundation for the existence of a single solution beneath a critical level of energy through a combination of the topological critical point theory and an appropriate change of variables technique. Furthermore, we demonstrate that multiple solutions exist when the energy reaches the double critical level by employing a mountain pass theorem within the context of the abstract critical point theory and a concentration compactness technique. Additionally, we provide nonexistence results for solutions with certain symmetries within the context of the Kirchhoff functional and the singular Trudinger-Moser growth condition.

We investigate the concentration behavior of functions of vectors whose entries are independent and draw from distributions that exhibit a weakened version of reverse concave properties. Under this distributional assumption and given a function that maps vectors to binary random variables, we establish the existence of a weakened version of the Talagrand inequality, which in turn allows us to demonstrate the existence of a constant C and properly defined norms ||.||, (?.), and (?.*) such that the following inequalities are met: C·(1+||.||_*)^r ·(1+||.||_*)^s ·(.|.|_.*) ≤ (1+.*)^t ≤ exp(C'(1+||.||_*)^r ·(1+||.||_*)^s ·(.|.|_.*) for some set of positive integers including r=s=t=1, and show that this leads to a weakened version of the Kahadikar-Khare-Mesnikov inequality, which further implies the strengthened version of the Baker-Erdős-Kalai conjecture, and also imply the strengthened version of the Baker-Erdős-Kalai conjecture for random variables, as well as a number of other concentration disparities including a number associated with Schramm-Anderson clusters, and others.

We establish that symplectic reductions, in the broad sense, encompassing the Poisson reduction and the symplectic reduction, correspond to the image of symplectic reductions under a specific group of transformations, known as symplectic modifications, under the natural equivalence relation. By analyzing a locally defined, differential multi-formality property, we are able to demonstrate the diversity of reduced spaces by exhibiting the images of constant symplectic modifications along the symplectic group. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the original and reduced spaces through the inverse of the reduction map, where the latter is found to be associated with the derivative of the reduction map when considered as a multi-vector field.

The suitability of kidneys for transplantation is evaluated on a case-by-case
basis, with medical professionals using their discretion to make judgments.
Studies have shown that, in the past, female kidneys were less desirable for
transplantation due to concerns about donor size and post-operative care,
although more recently, female kidneys have been found to function as well
as male kidneys in recipients of the same sex. Using data from the United
Network for Organ Sharing, we investigate how gender affects the outcome of
kidney transplantation and identify factors that influence graft survival in
men and women separately. Our study reveals that, although gender does not
affect graft survival in the long term, there are notable differences in the
short-term outcomes of men and women, with women experiencing higher rates of
graft rejection and acute rejection episodes. We also find that the ideal
acceptance of incompatible kidneys varies depending on the characteristics of
the donor and recipient. Specifically, it appears that female kidneys are more
suitable for female recipients than for male recipients. We further examine
the suitability of kidneys from older donors and those with proteinuria and
elevated blood pressure and find that they are less desirable due to lower
long-term survival rates. We also look at the effect of cold ischemia time and
find that it has a significant impact on post-transplant survival, with a one
hour increase in cold ischemia time associated with a 0.3 percent decrease
in one year survival

Recent advances in natural language processing, particularly with word embeddings, have been claimed to capture the nuanced semantic characteristics of financial reporting language. Researchers such as Loughran and McDonald have noted the special characteristics of financial text, including the consistent use of positive or negative word forms to convey emotions or opinions. Although various studies have validated some aspects of their findings, they have also questioned the universality of these text patterns. Our analysis reveals that the described phenomena are not exclusive to financial reporting but rather are inherent features of the English language. Words like "big" can express both large quantity and insignificant compared to "little". As a result, we argue that the distinctive properties of financial language are not a result of word embeddings capturing its unique semantics but rather a result of their general semantic capture capabilities. We have also experimented with a network that separately accounts for quantity and polarity, and our results show that it can effectively distill the underlying semantics from words, including those with polarized meanings.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based alternatives for a proposed integrated data and power transfer technology called broadband waveforming. In this technology, power and data are transmitted through distinct frequency bands to maximize energy transfer efficiency while minimizing interference with data transmission. Following the initial publication of broad waveforming in [1], these variants are advantageous as they offer similar benefits at a reduced cost. For SISO-OFDM, the energy transfer is enhanced by up to 75.8% compared to separate transmission of energy and data, with the performance being particularly notable in scenarios with insufficient light. For MISO-OFDM, the performance is examined under various COFDM/OFDM configurations, demonstrating the versatility of this technology.

This research introduces a novel mixed method for handling level sets and embedded boundaries in problem contexts like the one described, where a melting solid is subject to heat transfer. This technique bypasses the need to convert level set-based problems into conservation form. Instead, we employ a diverse approach to handle boundary treatment and level sets, utilizing the potential benefits of both methods. A numerical strategy based on finite elements is developed to solve these types of problems, and the efficacy of the approach is demonstrated through simulations of melting problems.

In multiagent competitions, players facing unknown opponents often learn
through trial and error, and the stability of learned behaviors depends on
the underlying strategy space. For general strategy spaces, including those
with multiple agents playing different games, we show that opponents' logs
can be effectively screened for rationalizable equilibria using a variety of
methods, including binary search and linear extrapolation. Our results also
include algorithms that directly yield a rationalizable equilibrium from
any set of opponents' logs and prove the correctness of these methods by
leveraging the concept of "strategically similar" log profiles. Furthermore
we demonstrate the practical feasibility of these methods through experiments
involving the learning of Nash equilibria in multiagent games such as grid
worlds and traffic scenarios.

An analysis of a stochastic model is presented, where a disease spreads among members of a society, with immune individuals reconnecting to others in the society through a process called "super spreader events". The model takes into account variations in the duration of immunity and the frequency of such events, and it demonstrates the model's ability to mimic patterns observed in real data. The researchers also discovered that a critical threshold exists, beyond which an outbreak is likely to occur even at very low disease transmission rates. This threshold is affected by the frequency of immune individuals reconnecting to others and the duration of their immunity, as well as other factors such as population size and the rate of super spreader events. The researchers further found that the model can exhibit indications of a second threshold, below which an outbreak becomes probable due to the prolonged duration of immunity, even if the population remains connected in a way that prevents an outbreak driven by reconnecting to others.

Integrating new data into the world-wide PDF4NLO collaboration has motivated the development of a theoretical framework that addresses fit objectives, data constraints, and regularization approaches within the context of an expansion in powers of $1/s$. This framework builds upon the foundations established by the PDF4NLO group and incorporates novel strategies for dealing with fit objectives, including the application of penalties. Additionally, predictions for observable quantities are generated through the development of analytical formulas in the context of the $k_{\perp}$-factorization framework. By leveraging the Monte Python framework, connections have been established with existing interfaces used for PDF fits.

To improve the effectiveness of experience replay, we propose a novel scheme
to select data for policy optimization by considering the variance of values
obtained from the same state. This method prioritizes transitions that lead
to a greater change in the value function for the same starting state, thus
more efficiently exploring the policy space and reducing the variance of value
estimates. We validate our proposed scheme through a series of experiments on
three discrete-action environments from the Gym platform and three continuousaction
environments from the Mujoco and D4M platform, achieving superior performance
to multiple baseline methods including standard priority replay.

In our analysis of human conversation, we observed that conversations frequently diverge from their original topic, with 63% of turns being significantly distinct from previous turns. To address this, we developed the MultiTalk model, which incorporates a highly branching mechanism allowing for diverse responses across multiple contexts. This model comprises three components: a context-aware neural response generator, a set of expert neural response generators for specialized contexts, and a controller to navigate between them. When testing the model, our results showed improvements over existing dialogue systems in terms of diversity, coherence, and overall satisfaction among users. Specifically, our model yielded a 19% increase in satisfaction related to diversity and a 25% decrease in dissatisfaction linked to coherence.

We've developed an efficient computational method for mimicking altered gravity models in N-body simulations using a conformally related metric. This approach leverages the equivalence between altered gravity and General Relativity within a conformally related spacetime framework. Through a key relationship between the scale factor and a set of "eta" parameters, we can replicate simulations of altered gravity on a conformally related spacetime in a calculable, fast manner. A previous study introduced this method and tested its validity within modified gravity models. In the present work, we expand upon the previous research by developing a range of simulated models based on altered gravity scenarios, including both generic and specific formulations such as $f(R)$ gravity and Brans-Dicke theory. An illustrative example demonstrates the method's capabilities by generating simulated data for the Brans-Dicke theory, which we then analytically match to predicted signals in altered gravity models. Our method allows for a rapid conversion between the conformally related and altered gravity spacetime formulations via a non-linear inversion technique. This approach enables the retrospective identification of simulated altered gravity models simply by analyzing the eta parameters of existing N-body simulations without the need for additional knowledge.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a highly structured database, allowing users to conduct advanced
queries, sort and prioritize content, and track changes, among other features.
This project aims to reengineer the wiki structure to meet the needs of
research collaboration, specifically in physics research, by incorporating
mathematical notation and advanced formatting capabilities.
Additionally, it plans to integrate multiple tools and platforms, such
as LaTeX, Python code, and graphical code executables, into the wiki for
easy reference and verification of equations.
The WorkingWiki prototype is presented as a customizable platform for
research collaboration, available on GitHub under an open-source license.

A novel approach has been presented that utilizes an active flame method to safely experimentally investigate the reaction of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic excitation within a linearized structure. The study's test arrangement, featuring a linearized steel plate and a combustion chamber, allowed for the position and intensity of acoustic waves to be controlled through the use of speakers. To prevent structural damage and ensure operator safety, flames were kept at a lower intensity than the minimum required for self-sustaining combustion. As such, a mechanism was developed to maintain combustion through the introduction of additional fuel. Following the development of this fuel injection system, measurements were taken of acoustic pressure and flame stability within various experimental configurations. The results showed that pre-existing pressure fluctuations could be delayed by counteracting pressure waves, achieved through the introduction of additional fuel. In turn, this led to increased fuel injection, which in turn resulted in flame stability. Furthermore, correlations were established between flame stability and both the amplitude and frequency of pressure fluctuations.

We investigate the impact of ultralight dark matter on neutrinoless double beta decay, considering the scenario in which a single neutrino interacts with a single ultralight dark matter particle through the Hubble expansion or gravitational acceleration within a decay nucleus. Due to the oscillations and CP phases, even if there are very small neutrino masses, extremely sensitive experiments may be needed to detect a signal above background. Ultra-light dark matter particles, with a mass range $10^{-25}$ to $10^{-7}$eV, would significantly impact the morphology of decay products. We show that the signal from a decay experiment, combined with external constraints and the absence of a signal from cosmological surveys, can pinpoint the mass and velocity dispersion of ultralight dark matter at the neutrino-source location.

We introduce a nonlocal gravity model based on the concept of essential tetrads, which allows for the description of gravity through the symmetrized trace of a tensor operator. By employing a constitutive connection approach, we derive a nonlocal Ricci tensor that connects the curvature tensor to the trace of a tensor operator. Through the use of essential tetrads, we redefine the nonlocal Ricci tensor in its simplified form. By incorporating a nonlocal Ricci scalar into the Einstein-Hilbert action, we obtain a nonlocal gravitational action. We then apply the Euler-Lagrange operator to the nonlocal Ricci scalar, which yields a nonlocal Poisson equation with a tensor operator. We solve this equation in both the local and nonlocal cases, first in a flat spacetime and then in a curved spacetime defined by a metric tensor. We then derive the nonlocal Einstein-Hilbert action through a variation approach, which yields the same results. We also explore the connection to polymeric gravity and point out the differences between the approach taken here and the standard polymeric gravity method.

Understanding the intricate relationship between genomics and function at a genome-wide scale holds significant value in pinpointing the functional implications of associations identified through genome-wide association studies. In this study, the association data of 18 traits was examined in conjunction with multiple types of genomics information, including epigenomics, transcriptomics, genetics of linkage disequilibrium, and genetics of ancestry, across multiple populations. The analysis revealed diverse patterns of association for the 18 traits across different regions of the genome, with associated regions concentrated in gene-rich areas for certain traits like Crohn's disease, whereas for traits like height, associated regions are predominantly found in gene-poor areas. Furthermore, certain associated regions were found for all 18 traits within specific regions such as downstream of genes, within genes, and promoter regions. The analysis of trait-specific patterns of association across different populations and genomic regions can facilitate a deeper comprehension of the underlying biology and potentially guide future studies, with results presented for 18 complex human characteristics including type-2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, melanoma, prostate cancer, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, heart disease, kidney disease, and Alzheimer's disease.

The discovery of Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed the existence of the fundamental scalar field predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics. However, within the Standard Model, there is an unsolved paradox known as the "hierarchy problem," which refers to the disparity between the extremely small size of fundamental particle properties and the large size of physical particle properties. To better comprehend this paradox, researchers focus on tiny systems that either mimic the characteristics of the vacuum or incorporate a fundamental scalar field, thereby providing insights into the hierarchy problem. This report delves into the findings from the 2019 and 2020 data-taking periods at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, presenting a comprehensive review of measurements related to the hierarchy problem, encompassing both the properties of the lightest known particle (the Higgs boson) and the vacuum energy of the Standard Model.

Observations indicate that some Galactic luminous low-mass X-ray binaries exhibit prolonged periods without activity. A subset of these, characterized by massive neutron stars and donors below 1.4 solar masses, exhibit narrow spectral spectra and show no signs of accretion within our observable range. The pattern of their X-ray outbursts, particularly the stable interval of their major bursts, hasn't been well understood until now. Based on current data and considering that these bursts are likely caused by the breakup of the star due to gravitational forces during its spin cycle, we can infer that these binaries have a narrow range of acceptable spin rates. For the most active ones, within the observed range, this range isn't wide enough to accommodate the observed interval of its bursts without assuming that its spin rate isn't constant. Furthermore, by analyzing the current data, we find that the pattern of its bursts isn't random, rather it follows a pattern that's likely caused by the change in its spin rate over time, specifically a decrease in its interval with each successive burst.

THz phonons in solids are not merely passive bystanders but instead influence the
behavior of electrons within materials. Research has shown that the impact of
phonons can be substantial, leading to the creation of novel states of matter,
and it is essential to consider their dynamic effect on electrons. However, the
magnitude of this impact is dependent on the specific conditions, being most
pronounced when a particular direction is aligned with a key symmetry element,
such as a crystallographic axis, a mirror plane, or an rotation axis.
Furthermore, this impact can manifest through either the coupling of a photon
with the oscillatory motion of electrons relative to the atomic framework or
with the spin precession generated by this motion. As a result, it will be shown
how essential it is to consider the dynamic electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interaction in solid-state materials physics, with a focus on
iridates and alpha-ruthenates as key examples.

Our analysis highlights the diversity of semantic variations within a sentence pair, drawing from natural language inference data. We distinguish between pairs exhibiting structural semantic differences, alongside various specific categories like lexical, relational, and contextual variations. By categorizing pairs in this way, we uncover the scope of semantic diversity and identify patterns of variation that NLI models struggle with, and show that these difficult instances are often related to ambiguous or misleading context. We further demonstrate the value of this framework in predicting the degree of semantic change and the success of NLI models in handling diverse sentence pairs. Our study provides a precise semantic characterization that can be utilized across NLI models and data, and with 50 diverse categories, we believe it suitable for a wide range of tasks and applications beyond NLI, including natural language generation and semantics-based retrieval.

We employed numerical methods to model rotating substellar objects with a composition of hydrogen, helium, and metal, based on the Mie-Grueneisen-Kutatani equation of state, up to their mass-shedding limits. Calculations were performed for a range of masses between 0.1 and 0.5 solar masses, with surface temperatures between 2000 and 5000K, and with various initial rates of rotation. Results show that for masses between 0.1 and 0.5 solar masses, the critical rotation rates required to prevent collapse decrease with increasing mass, until a break point at approximately 0.25 solar masses, where the relationship shifts to positive correlation with mass. Above this break point, the relationship between the angular momentum limit and mass becomes non-linear, influenced by inner layers of the star. For masses between 0.01 and 0.1 solar masses, the relationship between the angular momentum limit and mass remains linear, until a point where the star starts to shed its inner layers.

The analysis of amplitude data through fit functions is a useful tool for research, yet its potential limitations should not be ignored. By comparing actual data with fit functions, researchers can gain insights into underlying physical processes, as well as potential issues with measurements or equipment. However, such comparisons can take on complex forms that, when analyzed, may indicate issues with data collection but go undetected nonetheless. This paper will outline an alternative approach to amplitude analysis that produces distinct features in fit functions, making it easier to identify data collection problems or other anomalies in amplitude data.

A novel approach to modeling afterglows within a global framework is proposed, 
departing from the conventional separation into multiple phases. 
Instead, this approach leverages six key components to describe the dynamic 
afterglow progression. By comparing this framework's results with existing models, 
we demonstrate that it mimics the traditional three-phase model, albeit with some 
notable differences. Specifically, the novel framework's "early" phase occurs 
entirely within the radiative phase, whereas the "middle" phase begins once the 
adjoining components reach a state of balance. Furthermore, there is no sharp boundary 
between the "middle" and "late" phases, which instead meet at a logistic curve. 
This afterglow framework can be applied to both non-radiative and hybrid scenarios. 
It is worth noting that this afterglow framework can be used in conjunction with 
the global framework to analyze observed data, but with a more complex interpretation 
of the resulting components.

Bipartite graphs featuring two distinct groups of vertices have numerous practical applications, often requiring the separation of nodes within one class to minimize connections with the other class. This task is analogous to balancing a set of weights on a seesaw by placing masses on one side, where each mass represents a node from the opposing group and must be balanced with its counterpart from the same group. To achieve this balance, we can consider a variety of heuristics and exact methods, yet another perspective views the problem through the lens of a linear program that assigns weights to nodes from one class to represent the number of connections with the other class, thereby aiming to find the most balanced state. In the context of an instance with n nodes across two classes, we establish that the process of determining the most balanced state through weight assignments can be accomplished in time that scales with a polynomial of sorts, specifically O(n^3) when utilizing an interior point method to solve the linear program, or O(n^2) with a more direct approach.

Recently, studies on the biomechanics of human walking have been complemented by tests on catapulse, a proposed gait where each step is followed by a quick push forward. We have investigated catapulse with an emphasis on its potential benefits over traditional walking. By comparing the parameters of walking and catapulse, we found that the optimal stride length and period for catapulse are the same as those for walking, yet the optimal pace for catapulse is greater than the walking limit. Consequently, we discovered that catapulse is more resilient to external disturbances than walking. Furthermore, when modeling a simple pulse engine, we found that its power requirements for catapulse are lower than those needed for walking at the same speed.

Consider a field of fractions that is generated by a set of elements within a given field, provided those elements do not contain any denominator with the property of being a square in the given field's square root field. Then the ring of this fraction is considered and within it, a prime ideal is defined that does not contribute any information to the Krull dimension when paired with another ideal in the ring of symmetric polynomials over the square root field's coefficients. It is shown that this prime ideal's properties result in the ring being integrally closed and geometrically regular, and consequently, this implies the stability of the underlying field within certain algebraic and model theoretic frameworks.

Deep learning models have experienced rapid growth in size, making efficient deployment on limited resources a pressing concern. Our novel HyperDegrade NN (HDNN) framework targets large convolutional neural network models by intentionally narrowing their convolutional kernels. Contrary to traditional efficient CNN methods that focus on large filter sizes, HDNN deliberately uses small kernel sizes of 3x3 or 5x5 in specific layers to achieve a 2 times decrease in computational workload without sacrificing accuracy. Our research involves deliberately designing and testing narrow kernel CNNs to understand their behavior and identify key parameters that influence their performance. We apply the HyperDegrade framework to multiple tasks and models, resulting in a 23% reduction in MACs without accuracy loss for VGG, a 17% decrease in MACs with a 5x8 patch size for Transformer-based models, and a 2x reduction in MACs without accuracy loss for certain linear layers in ResNet.

A newly devised inductive method for untangling knots is presented, building on the principles of subdivide-and-recombine. This approach is particularly useful as it differentially distinguishes knotted structures, compared to the previously established method. As a result, the untangling process is significantly altered to accommodate a more complex pattern of branch division. Moreover, this approach can be applied to welded knots. Notably, a pattern of 16 distinct branch divisions was discovered, which serves as the foundation for an inductive method for untangling welded knots.

We've demonstrated that the Fox-Hatcher loop is a Vassiliev invariant of a specific order and it's linked to the Euler characteristic through a more intricate formula that incorporates the Vassiliev degree. This relationship was previously established by a different method in [6]. We've also derived a Vassiliev invariant of order three by utilizing the 1-cocycle that generates the universal cycle cocycle, and it's distinct from the Euler characteristic. This distinction holds when considering the Vassiliev degree.

In collaborative systems with multiple autonomous agents, optimal performance is achieved when tasks are assigned and coordinated among the agents based on their individual capabilities and those of their neighbors. This research explores the automated discovery of efficient strategies for collaborating robots in a complex environment by focusing on a conceptual framework of a knowledge base that represents the agents' capabilities and their spatial configuration. Through graph theory and mathematical optimization, a conceptual approach is translated into a tangible problem, and a meta-heuristic algorithm is developed to find high-performance solutions among which the ideal ones align with theoretical optimality benchmarks. Experimental evaluations in realistic scenarios, conducted using multiple simulation environments, demonstrate significant improvements in problem-solving when compared to existing competing methods.

In the context of a student information system that is part of a federated learning environment, an individual with significant influence can manipulate models locally to their benefit, despite privacy protections. This type of behavior, which we refer to as targeted model manipulation, allows the attacker to obtain valuable information from a student database that is supposed to be kept private, even after training on a small dataset for a limited number of iterations. We have discovered several ways an attacker may obtain this information, including through attacks that take account of variations in student demographics, identifications of individual students, or the disclosure of sensitive information about a student subgroup. The effectiveness and feasibility of these attacks are demonstrated in an actual scenario involving a small dataset from a university student system. We have discovered several ways an attacker may obtain this information, including through attacks that take account of variations in student demographics, identifications of individual students, or the disclosure of sensitive information about a student subgroup. The effectiveness and feasibility of these attacks are demonstrated in an actual scenario involving a small dataset from a university student registry. We have found various ways an attacker may obtain this information, including through attacks that take account of variations in student demographics, identifications of individual students, or the disclosure of sensitive information about a student subgroup. The feasibility of these attacks is demonstrated in an actual scenario involving a small dataset from a university student registry.

Kernel methods rely on kernels to capture data properties, yet traditional choices like the Gaussian kernel do so in an unspecific, data-independent manner. This limitation is particularly pronounced in applications where low-dimensional representations are used to analyze high-dimensional data, often showing poor performance due to data from different directions having distinct patterns. To address this challenge, we propose using random Fourier features as kernels, which become data-dependent that capture underlying patterns. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three datasets within the context of manifold learning and kernel density estimation.

Our novel approach, the Cartesian Decomposition Method (CDM), enables the automatic creation of syndicate functions for symmetric multi-processor optimization by embedding a function into a product of sub-functions. Initially, we conceived CDM to enhance Garand's method, which we expanded to handle complex scenarios involving multiple sub-functions. In response to Garand's concern for excessive node creation, we developed an efficient strategy to establish connections between nodes. By applying a topological sort and a priority-based ordering, we streamlined the process to a logical sequence of operations, thus directly producing the desired product structure without the need for a graph transformation. Our innovation facilitates easier return to the original domain, making it suitable for problem solvers that preserve the problem's original structure.

We establish that a compact hypersurface in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ with constant M\"obius curvature and satisfying specific symmetry properties is consistently geodesic and thus has constant scalar curvature within the conformally flat ambient space framework.

A new method is proposed to manage wireless resources in multi-service wireless systems that use simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT). The suggested approach, based on efficient threshold-based resource allocation, is compared to an existing scheme. It is shown that the proposed method results in significant increases in data transfer rate and significant gains in throughput and probability of successful data transfer, along with a minimal loss in transmitted power.

The Cayley graph of a function $f$ in $n$ variables serves as a representative model for a type of random walk called the embedded walk. It is essential to understand the structure of this graph, especially in the context of analytic combinatorics, as it influences the characteristics of the function's asymptotic behavior in the limit as $n$ approaches infinity. A key aspect of the Cayley graph is the appearance of periodic oscillations in the increments of its barycenter, which in turn affect the asymptotic distribution of the function's averages. To demonstrate the significance of these oscillations, we examine the asymptotic distribution of the average of $f_n$ for a specific choice of the function $f$, which exhibits power-law behavior resulting from the interplay between linear and quadratic components.

The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is limited by the noise generated from the motion of the sensing material by incident photons. To mitigate this limitation, the sensing material is positioned within the light cavity to take advantage of the amplified response to gravitational waves through the forward scattering of light. We analyze the performance of a light sensing cavity based on an interferometer with a specific design, known as sloshing-Sagnic, and compare it to an optical cavity using a dielectric mirror. Our results indicate that the noise from the motion of the sensing material can be significantly reduced by using an interferometer with a small mirror, and that a titanium alloy cantilever with a light-coated surface enhances the response to gravitational waves while minimizing noise from mechanical resonance. Based on the noise analysis, we estimate that a sloshing Sagnac interferometer with a titanium alloy cantilever would reach a frequency sensitivity of $3.3 \times 10^{-19}$ Hz$^{-1/2}$ around a frequency of 300 Hz.

Recent large-scale MIMO deployments are subject to performance limitations due to the growing number of users and devices. A key challenge is the increasing likelihood of overlapping visibility areas among users with half-duplex devices in stochastic access protocols like XL-MIMO. Our study examines the overlap zones and calculates the probability of users being in separate visibility areas, establishing a key performance indicator - the visibility area blocking probability (VBBP). By leveraging tools from stochastic geometry and probability theory, we derive an expressible VBBP formula and validate it through simulations. Our data suggests that the VBBP model accurately reflects real-world performance even with complex, randomized scheduling patterns.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized concentrations of material. Theoretical modeling suggests that the development of VSI leads to the creation of multiple substructures in the upper layers of protoplanetary disks. Utilizing simulations that account for VSI's effects on particles of varying sizes and their distribution across the disk, we have reconstructed detailed images of the electromagnetic spectrum. By conducting artificial data analysis on modeled images, our research provides specific predictions for: the detectability of substructures in the SED data; the most prominent features that should appear in images created through simulation; and the characteristics of features resulting from the accumulation of solid material. According to our findings, even with the current level of observational technology, it is possible to detect the electromagnetic radiation emitted by particles in the inner regions of disks with substructures shaped like spiral arms. The analysis of such features in simulated images suggests that the most prominent patterns in many disks take the form of multiple arm features, particularly in the 500 micron wavelength band.

New findings related to the "Big Apple" pattern - a recently discovered quark combination that forms a color-neutral system with the highest possible mass - hold significant promise in advancing quark combination and diquark models, potentially leading to a deeper understanding of confinement and the strong force. By incorporating the "Big Apple" pattern, researchers were able able to achieve remarkable consistency in calculations of quark combinations and scattering lengths within quantum chromodynamics. Furthermore, this achievement has been shown to extend to both infinite and finite temperatures. Additionally, research revealed that the "Big Apple" pattern contributes to the stability of neutron stars and places constraints on the mass of heavy quarks.

We demonstrate the versatility of frequency-tuned M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates within a motionally coupled system by showing that they remain resilient in the face of changing frequency ratios between multiple motionally connected modes. As long as the driving frequencies on one side are equal and the separation between the signal and the sideband frequencies elsewhere remains significant, our results indicate that these gates retain their coherence for an extended period - specifically, on the order of 100 times longer than the native dephasing time of a single mode. Furthermore, we found that exchanging the character of the motionally coupled mode from over-damped to critically damped does not significantly impact the durability of these gates. Our research shows that multiple motionally connected modes can function as a robust, high-q cavity by distributing coherence across them.

Our calculations predict that ZrGe and HfGe compounds exhibit unique electronic properties, featuring crossing points in their band structures and substantial spin-orbit coupling. These characteristics are rare in elemental materials but common in transition metal dichalcogenides with an in-plane direct gap. Our analysis indicates that these compounds possess significant interband electronic coupling and exhibit extreme anisotropy in their electron-phonon interactions, with an enormous effect on a high-frequency optical mode. This impact results in an extraordinary anomaly of the mode's frequency in relation to lattice parameters. Our findings also reveal that the electron-phonon interaction significantly affects the spin-orbit coupling, causing it to decrease with lattice parameter.
